entry: English actor. He played [[James Bond]] in seven Eon Productions films, from *Live and Let Die* (1973) to *A View to a Kill* (1985), more than any other actor in that series. On television he starred as Simon Templar in *The Saint* (1962–1969) and replaced [[James Garner]] as the lead of the American Western series *Maverick* (1960–1961). Moore was appointed a [[UNICEF]] Goodwill Ambassador in 1991 and was knighted in 2003 for services to charity. He received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2007.

English musician and songwriter. He co-founded [[Pink Floyd]] as its bassist in 1965 and was its principal lyricist and conceptual leader from 1968 until he left in 1985. Its concept albums include [[The Dark Side of the Moon]] (1973), [[Wish You Were Here (Pink Floyd album)|Wish You Were Here]] (1975) and [[The Wall]] (1979). His solo work includes *Amused to Death* (1992). Waters is a political activist who supports the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against [[Israel]]. Some of his comments and imagery have drawn accusations of [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]], which he has rejected as a conflation with anti-Zionism.

Interstellar object of planetary mass that is not gravitationally bound to any [[Star|star]] or [[Brown dwarf|brown dwarf]]. Also called a free-floating planet (FFP) or isolated planetary-mass object (iPMO), it may have been ejected from a planetary system or formed on its own. The [[Milky Way]] may contain billions to trillions of them. The first such objects were discovered in 2000 in the [[Orion Nebula]]. Celestial mechanics professor Cassidy Ward estimated the odds of one entering the solar system in the next 1,000 years at one in a billion.

Unusually large, unpredictable ocean surface wave. Also called a freak wave or monster wave, it is more than twice the significant wave height, which is defined as the mean height of the largest third of waves in a record. Rogue waves endanger ships and isolated structures such as lighthouses. They have no single distinct cause, but can occur when high winds and strong currents merge waves into one large wave. They are distinct from [[Tsunami|tsunamis]], which are long-wavelength waves caused by displacement of water, such as from earthquakes.

Game in which players assume the roles of characters in a fictional setting. Players act out these roles within a narrative, either through literal acting or through structured decision-making about character development, and actions succeed or fail according to formal rules. In the original tabletop form (TTRPG), play is conducted through discussion, and a game master (GM) decides the game system and setting and referees. In live action role-playing (LARP), players physically perform their characters' actions. Electronic forms include multi-user dungeons (MUDs), massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs) and single-player role-playing video games. Tabletop games may also be used in therapy to help people, including young people with neurodevelopmental conditions such as [[Autism|autism spectrum disorders]], ADHD and [[Dyslexia|dyslexia]], develop behavioral, social and language skills.

Recreational activity, sport and form of transportation in which people travel on surfaces with roller skates. Roller rinks and skate parks are built for it, though it also takes place on streets, sidewalks and bike paths. Roller skating originated in the performing arts in the 18th century, when skates were used on stage, possibly to simulate [[Ice skating|ice skating]]. Rubber wheels (1859) and four-wheeled turning skates (1863) helped it spread, and it boomed from 1880 to 1910. It was widely popular in the United States from the 1930s to the 1950s and again in the 1970s, when it was linked to [[Disco|disco]] music and roller discos. Inline skating became popular in the 1990s. Sport forms include [[Speed skating]], roller hockey, roller derby, [[Figure skating]] and aggressive inline skating.

American monthly magazine on music, politics and popular culture. Founded in San Francisco in 1967 by Jann Wenner and the music critic Ralph J. Gleason, it was first known for its coverage of [[Rock music|rock music]] and political reporting by [[Hunter S. Thompson]]. Its first issue featured [[John Lennon]] on the cover. It has been described as left-leaning and liberal. Wenner sold 49 percent to BandLab Technologies in 2016 and 51 percent to Penske Media Corporation in 2017, and Penske acquired the remaining stake in 2019.

Metal-forming process in which metal stock is passed through one or more pairs of rolls to reduce its thickness, make its thickness uniform, or impart a desired mechanical property. It is classed as hot rolling, above the metal's recrystallization temperature, or cold rolling, below it. Hot rolling processes more tonnage than any other manufacturing process. Rolling mills convert semi-finished [[Steel|steel]] castings into products such as structural steel, bar stock and rails. The earliest rolling mills, slitting mills, were introduced to England from what is now [[Belgium]] in 1590. Steam power, first recorded driving a mill in 1786, was displaced by electric motors soon after 1900. In 1783 Henry Cort received a patent for grooved rolls; his mills could produce 15 times more output per day than hammers, and he is called the "father of modern rolling".

Russian businessman and politician. He was governor of [[Chukotka Autonomous Okrug|Chukotka]] from 2000 to 2008 and is the former owner of Chelsea, a [[Premier League]] club in [[London]]. In partnership with Boris Berezovsky, he bought a stake in the oil company Sibneft in 1995 for about $100 million, well below market value. He sold it in 2005 for $13 billion. He is considered to have a good relationship with [[Vladimir Putin]], and after the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine he was made subject to sanctions because of these alleged ties.

State that dominated the Mediterranean and much of Europe, Western Asia and North Africa during the classical period. Its rule became permanently single-person after [[Augustus|Octavian]] was granted the title Augustus in 27 BC. The first two centuries of the Empire were known as the Pax Romana, and its territory reached its greatest extent under [[Trajan]] (r. 98–117 AD). A 50-year crisis in the 3rd century threatened its existence, and [[Diocletian]] later set up two imperial courts, in the Greek East and Latin West. [[Constantine the Great]] moved the imperial seat from Rome to Byzantium in 330, renaming it [[Constantinople]]. The [[Western Roman Empire]] collapsed in 476 AD, while the Eastern Roman, or [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]], Empire lasted until the fall of Constantinople in 1453. Its institutions and culture influenced language, religion, law and government for centuries.

Earliest period of Roman history, when the city and its territory were ruled by kings, c. 753–c. 509 BC. According to tradition, the kingdom began with the city's founding on the Palatine Hill beside the Tiber and ended when the kings were overthrown and the [[Roman Republic]] was established. Tradition names seven kings, and the last, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, is said to have seized power and ruled as a tyrant. Little is certain about the period, as few records or inscriptions from it survive. Accounts written during the Republic and Empire are thought largely to rest on [[Oral tradition|oral tradition]] and are debated as to their historicity.

Series of conflicts between Roman states and Iranian empires, from 54 BC to AD 628, beginning with the Roman Republic and the [[Parthian Empire]]. Much of the fighting involved vassal kingdoms and allied nomadic tribes, which acted as buffer states or proxies. Despite nearly seven centuries of hostility, the wars ended inconclusively. The border remained largely stable, although towns, fortifications and provinces were repeatedly sacked, captured and traded, and neither side could sustain lengthy campaigns far from its borders. By the 6th century the [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantines]] and [[Sasanian Empire|Sasanians]] were militarily similar and evenly matched. Their exhausted rivalry left both vulnerable when the [[Rashidun Caliphate]] launched the early Muslim conquests, which destroyed the Sasanian Empire and confined the Byzantines largely to [[Anatolia]] and southeastern Europe.

Polish and French filmmaker and actor. Born in Paris, he was taken to [[Kraków]] as a child. After [[Nazi Germany]] invaded Poland, his family was confined to the Kraków Ghetto, and his parents were taken in raids; he survived the Holocaust under a false identity. His films include *Knife in the Water* (1962), *Rosemary's Baby* (1968) and *Chinatown* (1974). He won the Academy Award for Best Director for *The Pianist* (2002). In 1969 his pregnant wife, the actress [[Sharon Tate]], was murdered along with four friends by members of the Manson Family. In 1977 he was arrested in the United States for drugging and raping a 13-year-old girl. He pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of unlawful sex with a minor, but fled the country before his 1978 sentencing and remains a fugitive from U.S. justice. Several women have since made allegations of abuse against him.

Period of classical Roman history, c. 509–27 BC, between the Roman Kingdom and the [[Roman Empire]]. Its government consisted of annually elected magistrates overseen by the Senate. Although there were elections, it was an elective oligarchy rather than a true democracy, with powerful families monopolizing senior offices. The Republic was in near-constant war. It defeated [[Carthage]] in the [[Punic Wars]], culminating at Zama in 202 BC, and became the dominant power in the Mediterranean world. Civil wars in the 1st century BC then broke the Republic. [[Julius Caesar]] and [[Pompey]] fought in 49 BC, and Caesar was assassinated in 44 BC. After [[Mark Antony]] and [[Cleopatra]] were defeated at Actium in 31 BC, the Senate granted [[Augustus|Octavian]] the title Augustus in 27 BC, which is often seen as the end of the Republic.

Art made in Ancient Rome and the territories of its Republic and Empire, including architecture, painting, sculpture and [[Mosaic|mosaic]] work. Sculpture was perhaps considered the highest form of art by Romans, and figure painting was also highly regarded. A very large body of sculpture survives from about the 1st century BC onward, but very little painting remains. Roman art is a creative pastiche that relied heavily on Greek models and also drew on Etruscan, native Italic and Egyptian visual culture. Many Roman sculptures known today are marble copies of Greek originals. Roman coins were an important means of propaganda and survive in enormous numbers.

Ruler of the Roman Empire, beginning with [[Augustus]] in 27 BC. Legitimacy depended on control of the army and recognition by the Senate. Succession was generally hereditary, but only if a candidate was acceptable to the army and bureaucracy. Early emperors presented themselves as leaders of the Republic. From [[Diocletian]] on, emperors ruled in an openly monarchic style. [[Constantine the Great]] moved the capital to [[Constantinople]] in 330 and was the first Christian emperor. The last Eastern emperor died in 1453, during the fall of Constantinople to the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottomans]].

Body of myths of ancient Rome, as represented in the literature and visual arts of the Romans. The Romans usually treated their traditional narratives as historical, even when they contained supernatural elements, and the stories often concern politics, morality and heroism. Ritual rather than myth was central to Roman religion, so some scholars have doubted that Rome had a native mythology, a view shaped by Romanticism and 19th-century classical scholarship. Roman myth drew on Italic traditions and, through the Hellenistic period and the conquest of Greece, on Greek mythology; the Romans identified their gods with Greek deities. Founding myths trace the city to the Trojan prince Aeneas and to the twins [[Romulus and Remus]]. Major sources include [[Virgil]]'s [[Aeneid]] and [[Ovid]]'s [[Metamorphoses]].

Additive numeral system originating in ancient Rome, written with seven letters of the Latin alphabet: I (1), V (5), X (10), L (50), C (100), D (500) and M (1000). A smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted, as in IV (4) and IX (9). The system has no zero. From the 14th century it was gradually replaced by the positional [[Hindu–Arabic numeral system]], but Roman numerals persist on clock faces, such as that of [[Big Ben]] (designed in 1852), and in year numbers and copyright dates. For example, 1776 is written MDCCLXXVI, as on the book held by the [[Statue of Liberty]].

Passionate attraction between two people, or the cultural idealization of such love. In [[Psychology|psychology]], romantic love is considered a motivation or drive, distinct from though related to attachment. The term has several definitions, which can contradict one another. Collins Dictionary defines romantic love as an intensity and idealization of a love relationship in which the other is imbued with extraordinary virtue and beauty, so that the relationship overrides all other considerations. The concept also represents individualistic choice in marriage and sexual partners, though it is rarely realized fully. People who experience little or no romantic attraction are called aromantic. The word derives from the Latin *Romanus*, and in the [[Middle Ages]] *romans* came to denote narrative verse about chivalry and love.

Languages that directly descended from Vulgar [[Latin]], forming the only living subgroup of the Italic branch of the Indo-European language family. The five most widely spoken by native speakers are Spanish (519 million), Portuguese (267 million), French (75 million), Italian (67 million) and Romanian (25 million). More than 900 million people speak a Romance language natively, mainly in the Americas, Europe and parts of Africa. Spread by European colonialism from the 15th century, French, Spanish and Portuguese are widely used as [[Lingua franca|lingua francas]]. All five of the most widely spoken are official languages of the [[European Union]]. Because the Romance-speaking area was traditionally a [[Dialect|dialect]] continuum, there is no unambiguous way to divide its varieties into separate languages.

Literary genre of narrative fiction focused on a developing romantic relationship between two or more characters, often concluding with an emotionally satisfying or optimistic ending. Precursors include Samuel Richardson's sentimental novel *Pamela* (1740) and the novels of [[Jane Austen]], which inspired Georgette Heyer. Heyer's first romance novel, *The Black Moth* (1921), was set in 1751. The British publisher Mills & Boon shifted toward romance fiction in the 1930s, and from 1957 its novels were distributed in North America by Harlequin Enterprises. Kathleen E. Woodiwiss's *The Flame and the Flower* (1972) was the first single-title romance published as an original paperback in the United States. Romance fiction became one of the largest segments of the global book market.

14th-century Chinese historical novel attributed to Luo Guanzhong. It covers events from the decline of the [[Han dynasty]] and the Yellow Turban Rebellion to the reunification of [[China]] under the Western Jin in 280. Drawing on Chen Shou's *Records of the Three Kingdoms* and earlier chronicles, it combines historical figures and events with fictional scenes and supernatural episodes. It gives particular moral and political weight to Liu Bei and Shu Han. The novel is one of the Four Great Classic Novels of [[Chinese literature]] and is arguably the most widely read historical novel in late imperial and modern China. Its literary influence in East Asia has been compared to that of Shakespeare on English literature.

Medieval European architectural style predominant in the 11th and 12th centuries, distinguished from the later [[Gothic architecture|Gothic]] style by its semicircular arches. It was the first pan-European architectural style since Imperial Roman architecture, and it combined features of ancient Roman and Byzantine buildings with local traditions. Its buildings are known for massive walls, round arches, sturdy pillars, barrel vaults, large towers and decorative arcading. The most significant are the great abbey churches, many still standing. Many were rebuilt in the Gothic style in prosperous areas such as England and Portugal, so the largest surviving groups are in less prosperous regions, including southern France, rural Spain, rural Portugal and rural Italy.

European art style from about AD 1000 until the rise of the Gothic in the 12th century, or later in some regions. The term was coined by 19th-century art historians, especially for architecture that retained Roman features such as round-headed arches, barrel vaults and apses. Romanesque art was the first style to spread across all of Catholic Europe, from Sicily to Scandinavia, and it drew heavily on Byzantine painting and the Insular art of the [[British Isles]]. High relief was the dominant sculptural mode, and tympanums were carved with monumental scenes such as Christ in Majesty and the Last Judgment. Stained glass became widely used. Portraiture hardly existed, and compositions usually had little depth.

Indo-Aryan ethnic group, traditionally nomadic and itinerant. Linguistic and genetic evidence suggests the Romani originated in northwestern regions of the Indian subcontinent, and their westward migration is believed to have occurred around AD 1000. They arrived in Europe around the 13th to 14th century, via the [[Balkans]], and their most concentrated populations are now in Central, Eastern and Southern Europe and in West Asia, mainly [[Turkey]] and Iran. In English they are widely known as Gypsies, a term considered pejorative by some Romani; the first World Romani Congress in 1971 voted to reject all exonyms. The Romani language is Indo-Aryan, with strong Persian, Armenian, Greek and South Slavic influence, and it has more than 2 million speakers across several dialects. Communities also live in the Americas, including an estimated 1 million Romani in the United States and 800 thousand in Brazil.
